title: Work, Energy, and Power
short_intro: Work is defined as the scalar product of force and displacement vectors, representing the transfer of mechanical energy. Energy is the scalar capacity of a physical system to perform work, while power measures the rate of doing work or transferring energy.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of work by constant and variable forces, kinetic and potential energy theorems, conservation of mechanical energy, and basic power problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Conservative and non-conservative force fields, line integrals of force, potential energy curves, stability of equilibrium, and work-energy relations in rotating frames and variable mass systems.

prerequisites: Newton's laws of motion and free-body diagrams
Vector algebra (dot product and line integrals)
Kinematics of rectilinear and curvilinear motion

concept_notes.heading: Work Done by Constant and Variable Forces
bullets: Work W is defined mathematically as the line integral of force F along a displacement path C: W = ∫ F · dr.
For a constant force, this simplifies to W = Fs cos(θ), where θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.
Work can be positive (θ < 90°), negative (90° < θ ≤ 180°), or zero (θ = 90°).

concept_notes.heading: Conservative Forces and Potential Energy
bullets: A force is conservative if the work done by it along a closed path is zero, or equivalently, if the work done is independent of the path taken.
For a conservative force field, F = -∇U, where U is the potential energy function.
Non-conservative forces, such as kinetic friction and air resistance, dissipate mechanical energy into thermal energy.

concept_notes.heading: Work-Energy Theorem
bullets: The net work done on a particle by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy: W<sub>net</sub> = ΔK = K<sub>f</sub> - K<sub>i</sub>.
This theorem is valid in both inertial and non-inertial frames provided pseudo forces are included in the net force calculation.
It provides a first integral of the equation of motion, simplifying problems where time is not explicitly required.

concept_notes.heading: Power and Efficiency
bullets: Instantaneous power P is defined as the scalar product of force and velocity: P = F · v.
Average power is the total work done divided by the total time interval: P<sub>avg</sub> = ΔW / Δt.
Mechanical efficiency η is the ratio of useful output power to total input power.

derivations.title: Work-Energy Theorem for Rectilinear Motion
derivations.conditions: Particle of mass m moving under the action of a net force F along a straight line.
steps: Start with Newton's second law: F = m (dv/dt).
Express acceleration using the chain rule: dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v (dv/dx).
Substitute into the force equation: F = mv (dv/dx), which rearranges to F dx = m v dv.
Integrate both sides from initial position x<sub>i</sub> (velocity v<sub>i</sub>) to final position x<sub>f</sub> (velocity v<sub>f</sub>): ∫ F dx = ∫ mv dv.
Evaluate the integrals: W = (1/2)mv<sub>f</sub><sup>2</sup> - (1/2)mv<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> = K<sub>f</sub> - K<sub>i</sub> = ΔK.

derivations.title: Relation Between Conservative Force and Potential Energy
derivations.conditions: 1D conservative force field where work done depends only on endpoints.
steps: Define the change in potential energy ΔU as the negative of the work done by the conservative force: ΔU = -W = -∫<sub>x<sub>i</sub></sub><sup>x<sub>f</sub></sup> F(x) dx.
Differentiate both sides with respect to the final position x<sub>f</sub> using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Rearrange to express force in terms of potential energy: F(x) = -dU/dx.

formula_sheet.name: Work done by a constant force
formula_sheet.variables: F = force vector, s = displacement vector, θ = angle between F and s
formula_sheet.conditions: Force must be constant in magnitude and direction

formula_sheet.name: Work done by a variable force (1D)
formula_sheet.variables: F(x) = position-dependent force, x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub> = initial and final positions

formula_sheet.name: Kinetic Energy
formula_sheet.variables: m = mass, v = velocity, p = linear momentum
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for speeds v << c (non-relativistic mechanics)

formula_sheet.name: Potential Energy (Gravitational - Uniform Field)
formula_sheet.variables: m = mass, g = acceleration due to gravity, h = height above reference level
formula_sheet.conditions: Near Earth's surface where g is constant

formula_sheet.name: Potential Energy (Spring)
formula_sheet.variables: k = spring constant, x = elongation or compression from natural length

formula_sheet.name: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
formula_sheet.variables: E = total mechanical energy, K = kinetic energy, U = potential energy
formula_sheet.conditions: Only conservative forces do work (no non-conservative dissipation)

formula_sheet.name: Instantaneous Power
formula_sheet.variables: W = work, t = time, F = force vector, v = velocity vector

formula_sheet.name: Work-Energy Theorem
formula_sheet.variables: W<sub>net</sub> = net work done by all forces, ΔK = change in kinetic energy

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force-Displacement Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of force F on the vertical axis versus displacement x on the horizontal axis for a variable force.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area under the F-x curve represents the total work done by the force during the displacement interval.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via numerical interpretation of irregular geometric shapes (rectangles, triangles) under force curves.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential Energy Curve (U vs x)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing potential energy U as a function of position x, including local minima, maxima, and inflection points.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Minima correspond to stable equilibrium (F=0, d<sup>2</sup>U/dx<sup>2</sup> > 0); maxima correspond to unstable equilibrium (d<sup>2</sup>U/dx<sup>2</sup> < 0).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to determine equilibrium points, turning points of motion, and bound/unbound states.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Work Done by Spring Force (Hooke's Law Experiment)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Linear plot of restoring force F versus displacement x for a helical spring.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the F-x line yields the spring constant k, and the triangular area gives the stored elastic potential energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions evaluating spring energy storage and elastic potential energy changes.

solved_numericals.question: A block of mass 2 kg is pulled across a frictionless floor by a constant horizontal force of 10 N for a distance of 5 m. Find the work done by the force and the final kinetic energy of the block, assuming it starts from rest.
solution_steps: Identify given values: F = 10 N, s = 5 m, θ = 0°, m = 2 kg, u = 0.
Calculate work done: W = Fs cos(0°) = 10 N × 5 m × 1 = 50 J.
Therefore, final kinetic energy K<sub>f</sub> = 50 J.
solved_numericals.answer: Work done = 50 J, Final Kinetic Energy = 50 J

solved_numericals.question: A conservative force in a 1D system is given by F(x) = -ax + bx<sup>2</sup>, where a and b are positive constants. Find the potential energy function U(x), taking U = 0 at x = 0, and determine the positions of equilibrium.
solution_steps: Use the relation F(x) = -dU/dx, which gives dU = -F(x) dx.
Integrate from 0 to x: U(x) - U(0) = -∫<sub>0</sub><sup>x</sup> (-ax + bx<sup>2</sup>) dx = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>x</sup> (ax - bx<sup>2</sup>) dx.
For equilibrium, F(x) = 0 ⇒ -ax + bx<sup>2</sup> = 0 ⇒ x(bx - a) = 0.
Equilibrium positions are x = 0 and x = a/b.
solved_numericals.answer: U(x) = \frac{1}{2}ax^2 - \frac{1}{3}bx^3; Equilibrium at x = 0 and x = a/b

solved_numericals.question: An elevator of mass 500 kg is ascending with a constant upward acceleration of 2 m/s<sup>2</sup> over a height of 10 m. Calculate the total work done by the tension cable on the elevator. (Take g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
solution_steps: Apply Newton's second law for the elevator: T - mg = ma ⇒ T = m(g + a).
Substitute values: T = 500 kg × (9.8 + 2) m/s<sup>2</sup> = 500 × 11.8 = 5900 N.
The displacement s = 10 m upwards, in the same direction as tension.
Calculate work done by tension: W<sub>T</sub> = T · s = 5900 N × 10 m = 59,000 J.

assumptions_and_limitations: Classical mechanics assumes macroscopic particles where quantum uncertainty in position and momentum is negligible.
Potential energy is defined only for conservative force fields; non-conservative systems require tracking thermal energy dissipation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Work is always positive if a force is applied and an object moves.
common_misconceptions.correct: Work can be negative if the force component opposes the direction of displacement (θ > 90°).
common_misconceptions.why: Work is a scalar product taking into account the relative angle between force and displacement vectors.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centripetal force does zero work, so it can change the speed of a particle in circular motion.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centripetal force does zero work because it is always perpendicular to instantaneous displacement, hence speed remains constant in uniform circular motion.
common_misconceptions.why: W = Fs cos(90°) = 0, so by the work-energy theorem, kinetic energy and speed do not change.

quick_revision: Work is the area under the F-x curve and represents energy transfer.
The work-energy theorem equates net work to change in kinetic energy.
Conservative forces satisfy F = -dU/dx and path independence.
